text:
Alex Rivera: hey team, flagging an escalation — customer on Dedicated says they suddenly hit a bunch of 429s even though they were told burst credits would cover short spikes. billing page shows they still have some credits. can someone explain why they saw rejections and what we can tell them?

Maria Chen: quick summary — burst credits are separate from sustained quota. they smooth small bursts automatically but they also have a cooldown/regen window. if traffic is sustained beyond the smoothing window the system will start enforcing the soft quota -> 429s. did they have a prolonged spike or many concurrent callers?

Alex Rivera: looks like their traffic pattern: a 6-minute spike with many concurrent requests (hundreds of parallel). they thought "short" = a few mins. they expected credits to just soak it up.

Tim O'Neill: +1 — important nuance: burst credits help with short, transient spikes at *token* level and with small concurrency bursts. they don't magically raise concurrency limits. there's also per-route concurrency caps and per-account rate limits that can trigger before credits are exhausted.

Ingrid SRE: dropping the checklist we use when this comes up:
1) check account burst balance in Console -> Billing -> Burst credits.
2) check per-route quota and per-account concurrency in Console -> Usage -> Limits (or via API).
3) review request pattern (qps vs concurrency vs token/sec).
4) look at any smoothing config the customer set (burst smoothing, window sizes).

Maria Chen: here's a quick repro command to show their recent spike (we ran this for them):
```bash
# pull 1h of token-level aggregated usage for account_id=acct_123
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \
  "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/usage?account=acct_123&granularity=60m"
```
output we saw (abridged):
```
timestamp,requests,concurrency_avg,tokens
2026-11-02T13:10:00Z,1200,240,450000
2026-11-02T13:11:00Z,4200,980,1620000
2026-11-02T13:12:00Z,5300,1500,2200000
```
that 13:11-13:13 window is > a couple minutes of heavy concurrency. burst credits can't sustain that rate.

Jason - CS: customer-facing explanation we can use: "Burst credits are intended for short, transient spikes in traffic and token usage. They smooth brief bursts and help avoid immediate throttling. If traffic remains elevated for longer than the smoothing/cooldown window or exceeds concurrency caps, our platform will enforce rate limits to protect other tenants. To avoid future rejections you can either reduce concurrency in the caller, enable request queuing/smoothing on your side, or work with us to add temporary reserved capacity."

Alex Rivera: they asked if credits "regenerate faster" if they pause traffic. what's the official guidance on cooldown/regeneration?

Ingrid SRE: regen is time-based with a max replenish rate. short answer: credits recover slowly (minutes to hours depending on the account tier and how many credits were consumed). there's also a soft-cooldown where the system will still rate-limit until the moving average drops below threshold. we should avoid promising instant refill.

Tim O'Neill: operational fixes we recommended:
- set a client-side smoothing buffer: cap concurrency, use exponential backoff + jitter
- enable server-side smoothing (Console -> Traffic -> Burst smoothing): extend the smoothing window from default 30s to 120s for this workload if they need longer tolerance
- if spikes are regular, propose Dedicated reserved capacity increase or a scheduled scaling policy

Maria Chen: added a short-term remediation we can run for them: manual top-up of N credits (we can grant a one-off emergency credit) or temporarily raise their soft quota for 30m while they run a rollout. requires approval from billing ops.

Alex Rivera: customer asked for step-by-step to avoid this: can we give a short checklist they can follow?

Jason - CS: copy-paste checklist for customer: 
1) throttle concurrent callers to <= 200 (or whatever safe concurrency per their plan).
2) enable client-side queue with 100ms base delay + jitter.
3) configure server smoothing window to 60-120s in Console.
4) if you expect >10x baseline bursts more than 2 min, open a support ticket to request temporary reserved capacity or credit top-up.

Support Bot: automated note: ticket #S-38921 created and linked to account acct_123. escalation label: billing/credits. assigned: Jason - CS.

Ingrid SRE: I'll also run a quick ingestion check to confirm there were no runtime errors that exaggerated the counts (e.g., retries doubling traffic). if we see retries flooding, that may explain why they hit concurrency caps faster than expected.

Alex Rivera: perfect. I'll send the customer the explanation + checklist and offer a one-off credit while ops reviews. thanks everyone :thumbsup:

Maria Chen: FYI — we should add a short FAQ blurb to the docs about "Why did I get 429s even though I had burst credits?" with examples of traffic patterns that will still be limited. small docs task for devex.

Tim O'Neill: +1. can someone create a docs PR with the graph we used above? that visual really helps.

Jason - CS: taking actions: message to customer sent, ticket updated, cherrypick for emergency credit requested. I'll post outcome here later.

Alex Rivera: closing loop when ticket resolved.
